The reason why the second interpretation is not exclusively favored among the two is that the primary purpose was to establish the preceding section as the formal teaching (dharmatā) and the subsequent as the propagation (pravartana); this is merely a provisional approach.

Regarding the statement in the response, "The *Avataṃsaka* assembles the multitude in various places," and so forth: the specific locations and assemblies are fully detailed as cited in the *Shiqian*. In each assembly location, there is first the introduction followed by the main body; the meaning of the adornment of the dwelling place corresponds to the introduction.

Regarding the phrase "assembling the multitude," as seen in the "Chapter on Sublime Adornments," the "Chapter on Names and Titles," the "Chapter on Radiant Enlightenment," and each of the individual assemblies, the multitude is first assembled; this is intended to clarify that a single sutra possesses many distinct introductory sections.
The phrase "the *Āgama* sections are thus" clarifies that many sūtras share a common introductory formula.

In those four *Āgamas*, numerous short and long sūtras are each combined into a single collection (*nikāya*). Each individual short sūtra does not exceed one or even half a page, with the sole exception of the "Traveling Sūtra" (*Cankī-sutta*) within the *Dīrgha Āgama*, which alone comprises two fascicles.
Furthermore, there is a *Mahāvaipulya-sūtra* consisting of a single fascicle, wherein each individual sūtra is preceded by five thematic meanings.
Since the term "Āgama" serves as the general title for the collection, the minor sūtras within this division are designated as chapters (*pīṇḍa*).

Regarding the "Pre- and Post-scripts of Entrustment in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*": this clarifies that within a single scripture there are multiple sections of circulation; thus, the "Chapter on Successive Teachings" (*Ānuśāsana-parivarta*) in the second fascicle constitutes the pre-script of entrustment, while the "Chapter on Entrustment" (*Parīndanā-parivarta*) in the twenty-seventh fascicle constitutes the post-script of entrustment.
In accordance with those three sutras, what harm is there in having two prefaces?
Regarding the statement "the five meanings are not established," this explains the anticipated objection.
The objection states:
If that is so, why is this not the same as those *Āgamas*?
Should the present "Root Chapter" (*mūlaparivarta*) also be established in such a manner?

To explain the intent: although it is asserted that the Root Chapter of the present sutra is not the very beginning, one must further resolve the difficulty regarding the *Āgamas*. While the *Āgamas* mostly consist of general introductions (*pūrvayoga*) and the Root Chapter should likewise be so, because the *Āgamas* also include distinct sutras, they are not the primary beginning; thus, the five matters may still be established therein.
Since this present sutra is a single, unified scripture, there are only distinct [teachings] and no common ones; therefore, we take the *Avataṃsaka* as our precedent.

Thus, while the dependent origination in the *Āgamas* is distinct for each [text], the dependent origination in this present sutra is not different; for this reason, the five meanings are not established in the Root Chapter.

Regarding the statement, "The Trace Gate (jimen) consists only of the single section on circulation": when viewed from the perspective of the Trace in relation to the Origin (hon), and when the Origin is used as an analogy for the Trace, the Origin Gate is not the beginning and thus has a separate introduction; the Trace Gate is not the end and thus consists only of the circulation. Therefore, it contains only the exhortation to uphold [the teaching], but lacks the entrustment (zokurui).

Therefore, from the "Dharma Master" chapter to the "Peaceful Practices" chapter, there are five chapters in total that clarify the profound merit of propagating the sutra to encourage its circulation.

If, within the Fundamental Gate, one first takes the latter five chapters and excludes three and a half chapters as an exhortation to uphold and circulate [the teaching], then from the "Supernatural Powers" chapter onwards there are eight chapters that clarify the entrustment for circulation. Since the sutra was not yet concluded after the Trace Gate, it was neither a matter of circulation nor was there yet a need for formal entrustment.
Regarding the phrase "thus it is said," it shall be explained according to the subsequent commentary on the text.

As for the "explanatory glosses" (*tiēshì*), even the current general method of interpreting the sutra differs from various other views; how much more so does the *Lotus Sūtra* section differ from all other sutras? Therefore, each and every phrase is interpreted through four meanings. Yet, fearing that future readers might not comprehend these four meanings, I have preemptively provided a fourfold analysis of these four meanings.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the meaning": when it comes to the time of analyzing the text, perhaps four interpretations are not fully provided, but only one or two are retained, while the others are to be inferred.

Next, in explaining the reason for the four meanings, the first concerns the intent of the question: if it were abbreviated, there would be only one; if expanded, it would be immeasurable. Since neither the extensive nor the abbreviated approach would suffice, [the fourfold method is adopted].
"Fei" means "not so. For what reason are there only these four explanations?

In the answer, a single passage contains two meanings: first, it generally clarifies the reason for the four meanings; second, it clarifies the specific reason for each of the four. Both meanings are taken as being "moderate": first, there are only four, neither more nor less.

Next, following the section on "causes and conditions," it is clarified that each [factor] is neither lost nor deviant; therefore, although "one" occupies the middle position, it must still proceed to "four. Since the meaning is complete within the inclusion of "four," there is no need to exceed this number.
Even if one were to exceed this, it would still be subsumed within the four meanings; thus, both "four" and "one" are termed "occupying the middle."

As in the case of the ten wonders (*daśa-prakāra-vicitra*), each individual wonder also possesses the four intentions; even though the ten are included within the four, they are still termed "intermediate. Now, since we require only these four, they are called "intermediate," which is why the first intention states that "broad" implies "equal."

If one lacks this initial intention, one is no different from non-Buddhist schools; how much more so when the language of "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya) pervades the entirety of a single transformation—from the hells at its beginning to the Buddha-realm at its end, encompassing all that is sudden or gradual, and all teachings and flavors in between. Therefore, one must know that the four *siddhāntas* (fourfold truths) of this great matter are not for any other kind of response or stimulus. The four *siddhāntas* that reveal and manifest the One Path have nothing beyond them; the four *siddhāntas* of the long distant past are not found in other sutras; and the four *siddhāntas* of contemplating the mind are fully subsumed within a single contemplation. The four [truths] regarding persons and principles may be understood by analogy with these explanations.

These four *siddhāntas* (purposes) apply throughout from beginning to end; likewise, the three categories such as the "teaching" (*jiao*) must also be explained exhaustively, the intent of which can be understood.

If there were no sequential intent, one could not distinguish between the partial and the small [vehicles]. Therefore, by means of the four and eight [categories] to simplify and clarify the provisional and the ultimate, and by looking back at the teachings of the former divisions, it is now seen that these are truly real. Since all expressive designations no longer have different names, it is necessary to elucidate this to manifest the wondrous scripture. Without this third intent, who would know that it transcends all else?

Regarding the discussion of the bodies and lands within the teachings of a single dispensation, everything from the intermediate period up to the present day is nothing but a provisional manifestation (*jise*). To point to that Great Universal [Dharma] is like referring to a journey of two nights; yet, having first been deluded by the Esoteric Teachings and subsequently confused regarding the provisional body, it is only now that these attachments are dispelled. If one still remains mired in "clinging to the stump" and ignorant, how can one distinguish the merit of the expressive teachings without recourse to the fourth intention?
How then can this serve as the foundation for long-term practice?
Therefore, every single phrase enters the mind to form contemplation.
Thus it is said: "Contemplation accords with the sutra; it is not like counting another's treasures."
Only then will one realize that the single work, *Mohe Zhiguan*, is the fishing trap for the Lotus Samādhi.
If one grasps this meaning, one will finally comprehend the purport of the sutra; by synthesizing these four meanings, one can briefly reveal the ultimate aim of the entire treatise.
Therefore it is said: "If abbreviated, the meaning will not be comprehensive. One should know that even two or three [meanings] are still abbreviated; how then could one suffice?

To reach a middle ground, four meanings are established so that the significance is easily understood. Thus, each and every phrase possesses these four meanings, which ensures that every phrase differs from all other teachings. Consequently, the meaning of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is truly not difficult to grasp; hence it is said to be "easily understood."
Following the section on "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*), there is a detailed explanation of each point individually. Within this, the first part concerns causes and conditions;
the next section, beginning with "If in the ten directions," concerns the provisional teaching (*yāna*);
and the subsequent section, beginning with "If responding to capacities," concerns the fundamental and the trace (*honji-suijaku*).
Next, the section beginning with "If one seeks" concerns the contemplation of the mind.

Regarding the first [of the three] causal conditions: the initial passage provides the formal explanation, from the opening words "Thus have I heard" down to the conclusion "and departed. Since every part is nothing other than the true interaction between response and stimulus, we know that the response and stimulus of this sutra are wondrous.

Prior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, those of the Small Vehicle and those with dull faculties lacked the capacity for enlightenment entirely; though the principle was present, they were deluded, and thus it is said that although [the teaching] was near, they did not see it because their capacities had not yet been awakened to accord with it.
Compassion that extends from beginning to end is called the power of the roots of goodness; because phenomena and principle differ, it is termed "remote.
Because they meet without premeditation, it is said to be "spontaneous penetration.

Thus, prior to this, the wondrous Way had not yet intersected with response; the differences among the various schools, the superiority or inferiority of their teachers, and the differing gradual or sudden dispensations for sentient beings—all of these, one by one, are nothing other than the intent of responsive resonance.
Although they are collectively termed "response and resonance" (ganying), their manifest benefits are not yet universal;
although they are collectively termed the "four all-inclusive methods" (sishixi), there are distinctions of shallow and deep.
Whether combined or individual, their scope varies and lacks uniformity; it is only upon reaching the *Lotus Sūtra* that they finally become a single flavor.
Regarding the statement "there is no causal connection," this is countered by explaining that what was previously non-existent now exists.

From the phrase "roots of goodness of kindness and compassion" (*karuṇā-kuśalamūla*) onwards, it correctly clarifies that [the Buddha] exists because of present retribution; therefore, one should cite the distant past to demonstrate comprehensively that time is not out of sequence. Since the compassion without object (*apraṇihitā maitrī*) is all-pervasive, why would there be a distinction between the distant and the near?

It is simply that where there is no affinity, one is said to be distant; yet where there is resonance, there is necessarily penetration. The Buddhas do not come and sentient beings do not go; because the stimulus and the response correspond to one another, it is called the "intercourse of the Way."

Regarding the power of the root of goodness of compassion (*maitrī-kuśalamūla-bala*), while the general characteristics are the same, the specific details are briefly as cited in the sixth fascicle of the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe Zhiguan), which quotes the fourteenth chapter, "The Chapter on Brahma-conduct" (*Brahmacarya-paṭala*), of the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. Since the supernatural transformations (*ṛddhi-prātihārya*) of all Buddhas have compassion as their foundation, all dharmas are established by means of compassion.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: "If anyone should ask what is the root of all dharmas, one should say it is loving-kindness.
Thus, through response and resonance, all dharmas are subsumed.

Next, regarding the passage beginning with "Now, as for sentient beings," the intent of the inquiry is this: since it was stated that the four meanings constitute the "middle way," yet even the single meaning of "causes and conditions" involves a manifold of capacities and responses—its scope being even more extensive—how can it be called the "middle"?
The meaning is similar to "exceeding four," which is why it is called "furthermore" (*geng*).
As for what is meant by "the multitude," it refers to the five vehicles, the nine realms, and so forth.

Next, regarding the intent of the answer in the passage beginning with "The Great Sutra": since even four are still within the middle range, how could one [vehicle] being extensive be considered a discrepancy?

Therefore, within the broad sense of the term, it is also called "abiding in the middle. Thus, citing the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, although the gateways are immeasurable, they are all subsumed within supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). Supernormal power is simply another name for "response" (*ying*); it is so named because it corresponds to the "stimulus" (*gan*), constituting the relationship between stimulus and response.

However, the name and meaning of "supernatural powers" (abhijñā) apply to both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, whereas the term "responsive resonance" (yinggan) is restricted solely to the Mahāyāna; within the Mahāyāna, it pertains to stages from the first bhūmi upward, and in this present context, it refers precisely to the functioning of the ultimate fruit.

Therefore, the designation "supernatural power" (shentong) subsumes all under a single name; since it can still be called "concise," how could its meaning not occupy the middle ground between the extensive and the concise?

Since this is the case for that which responds, the same principle applies to that which is responded to. Thus, although the responses may be numerous, they do not exceed compassion; and although those seeking liberation may be many, how could they go beyond being moved [by it]? Therefore, it is clear that the two characters "response" and "inducement" (yinggan) occupy the middle ground.
Next, regarding the passage beginning with "If [one considers] the ten directions," first, within the context of the teaching (*jiao*), the author raises a broad objection;
next, with the passage beginning "Now, in this treatise," he explains the position of the middle way (*madhyama-pratipad*).

First, as for raising the objection: although the two terms "response" (*ying*) and "stimulation" (*gan*) are themselves situated in the middle when discussing the general matter of transformative activity, the teachings of the ten directions and the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are even more extensive. Thus, if one were to rely solely on the teaching, the position of the middle way would not be established.

Regarding the subsequent explanation: the present treatise concerns the Sahā world, which receives only the teachings of sound (*śabda-dharma*). Although it possesses both exoteric and esoteric elements—whether manifest or latent—it is termed "central" when compared to other lands. This further clarifies that the locus of resonance and response for the aforementioned teachings of sound is situated in this middle position.

Regarding the phrase "then the gate of ambrosia opens": this indicates that words merely serve as sounds for the benefit of others. Thus, the true aspect (*dharmatā*) is the ambrosia, while all teachings are its gates. These gates have no opening or closing, and this principle is neither passable nor obstructed; those who enter this land do not require other sensory objects, for they penetrate the principle through these [teachings], hence it is said that "the gate opens."

Regarding the phrase "relying on the teaching," it should properly be called "the teaching of sound" (*śabda-śāsana*); however, this is merely an abbreviation. Although there are physical scriptures (*rūpa-sūtra*) existing after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa—even those subsumed under the aggregates of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*), as well as the fragrant food of Vimalakīrti and the awakening through contemplation of the Dharma-practice—all of these take the golden-mouthed teaching of sound as their foundation. Since they are neither more nor less than this, the point is made clear.
Regarding the provisional and the ultimate (honji-suijaku), first, the extensive refutation of objections is presented;
next, from "From the necessity of establishing the finger" onwards, the exposition of the middle way is revealed;
and finally, from "Therefore, Zhao... onwards, the testimony of Sengzhao is cited to establish the proof.

Regarding the first passage: when responding to capacities, one cites the preceding causes and conditions; when establishing the teaching, one cites the preceding provisional teachings. Since capacities are manifold and teachings are diverse, their manifestations must necessarily be extensive; one should know that the "original" and the "traces" are not termed "central."

If one follows the statement regarding the "opening of the gate," then it is only the Perfect [teaching] that occupies the middle position, as already explained previously. Now, considering the interval between the fundamental [truth] and its traces—wherein today’s verbal teachings and their responsive resonance have opened and then been further bestowed, and having been abolished, are once again established—it is therefore called "expedient means and reality."

If even a single lifetime is already vast, how much more so after the ultimate realization has been achieved? Within that period, there are various distinctions in the manifestations of the teaching according to the capacities of those to be converted.

Regarding the terms "shallow" and "deep," while the principles of the provisional and the real are fixed, the meanings of shallow and deep are pervasive; therefore, they are stated twice for emphasis.

Next, to clarify the "position in the middle": previously, when comparing the vocal teaching (śabdopadeśa) to the response to resonance (prati-saṃvedana), the Sahā world was set in contrast to the ten directions; thus, the meaning of the Sahā world’s vocal teaching occupying the central position is fully established.

Now, as we wish to discuss the One Essence (tattva), we must address its many manifestations (vyañjana). Although these manifestations are numerous and vast—just as pointing at the single moon results in many reflected images—how could the fact that there are four fingers capable of pointing mean that the single moon being pointed at is not one?
Therefore, it is clear that the traces have been set aside to seek the original source.
As for the subsequent citation of Sengzhao, I merely borrow his words without adopting his views.
Since Sengzhao employed the "Nine Turns" of Master Daorong, and those Nine Turns were not yet correct, how can one who cites them be considered right?

Therefore, his *Benji wusheng che* (The Record of the Non-arising of the Fundamental and the Traces) states: "Prabhūtaratna does not perish and Śākyamuni is not born; Prabhūtaratna is the fundamental, and Śākyamuni is the trace.
The fundamental does not perish and the trace is not born; though the fundamental and the traces differ, their non-arising and non-perishing are inconceivably one."
"How can the root of Prabhūtaratna be made to descend through the traces of Śākyamuni?
If one uses the former to manifest the latter, taking the long-ago as the root and the present as the trace, then although the root and the trace differ, they are inconceivably one."
Next, regarding the explanation of contemplating the mind (*cittānupaśyanā*), it first raises and extensively analyzes the faults;
then, with the words "next, merely contemplate," it correctly clarifies the middle way.
First, the three preceding points concerning the investigation of traces and so forth involve understanding without practice—what benefit is there for oneself or others?

Because its traces pervade the ten directions, it is called "vast"; because its origin points back to the very beginning, it is called "lofty. To seek only the loftiness and vastness of another's fruit—what benefit is there for the comprehensiveness and depth of one's own cause?

If one takes faith and practice as one's vehicle and understands that [the Buddha] dwells eternally with a remote lifespan, what is there that is improper in seeking out his lofty and vast [qualities]?

It is only because the teachings are established to reveal the fundamental reality so that one may accord with the principle; therefore, failing to accord with this principle is called "counting another's treasure."

The verses of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* are fully explained in the *Zhiguan ji* and the *Shiqian*; however, because one contemplates the mind, one penetrates the loftiness and profundity of one’s own mind, thereby seeing its fundamental nature (*ben*).
Because one encompasses all through principle (*li*), one penetrates the vastness and comprehensiveness of one’s own mind, thereby seeing its phenomenal traces (*ji*).

Because a single thought-moment arises and penetrates to the very bottom of true reality (*dharmatā*), it is called "high"; because it is fully endowed with all phenomena (*dharma*), it is called "vast.
Furthermore, because it is the provisional (*upāya*) while being the ultimate (*paramārtha*), it is called "high"; because it is the ultimate while being the provisional, it is called "vast."

If it were not for this contemplation, one would merely experience the responses of the preceding three; thus, the provisional teachings would have to be opened up and the expedient fruits would have to be discarded. Consequently, the teachings being applied to the assembly would be termed "having an end," and the expedient contemplation would require alteration as the capacity [of the practitioner] would not be a response to the Sublime. Therefore, when the capacity is perfected, it has the power to evoke a response; when the contemplation is perfected, one enters the stage where one's own benefit is realized rather than that of others. For this reason, the contemplative mind possesses the aforementioned three meanings. Moreover, since there is a basis for entering the stage and the establishment of teachings through the manifestation of traces, how could these three meanings not be employed when they are fully present?

Therefore, when observing the mind as being in the middle, although the four intentions arise from one another in succession—with each preceding one being "extensive" and each succeeding one being "middle"—they are all nonetheless termed "middle" so long as they remain within their own respective domains.

Therefore, although these four intentions differ in name according to their application, they should be understood as progressively entering from the latter into the former; taken collectively, they do not exceed the principle of response and stimulus (*ganying*).

However, the reason the first is specifically termed "response and stimulus" is that we temporarily set aside the general for the particular, as the lower three lack the distinction between the coarse and the subtle. Thus, while the shallow and deep levels of the four *siddhāntas* remain undifferentiated, it is only through the teaching of the Voice (*śabda*) that one can distinguish the response and stimulus of the provisional and the real, which ultimately converge in the merit of the Perfectly Ultimate Teaching.

Although one knows that the ultimate perfection is fully contained within this present sutra, people remain obscured by long-standing habits and thus lose sight of its source. If one were to sweep away these manifested traces, all would descend from the fundamental source; yet, within the manifestation of response and stimulus, there is precisely the response and stimulus of the fundamental ground. The fundamental and the manifested are nothing other than a single, wondrous, lofty, and vast reality. Although one knows that the realization of this lofty and vast capacity arises through contemplation, once contemplation is perfected, there is a true response to the stimulus.

Thus we know that response and resonance (ganying) pervade the [final] three [stages]; how much more so when each stage successively encompasses the others? Although in principle they mutually encompass one another, in practice they must be clearly distinguished.
Regarding "the three citations of evidence": the first proves response and resonance;
the section beginning with "Furthermore it says" proves the characteristics of the teaching (jiaoxiang).
Below "Life Span," the fundamental and the trace are authenticated;
below "Simile," the contemplation of the mind is authenticated.
In the initial passage, there is first a citation; from "If a human or deva... onwards, there is an explanation.

The initial mention of "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) is simply another name for "response and stimulus" (*ying-gan*); since the names differ while the meaning remains the same, it serves as proof. However, because the term "causes and conditions" is general and not restricted to the relationship between agent and object, the *Zhi guan* (Mo-ho chih-kuan), fascicle 1, states:

"Either taking the sage as the cause and the ordinary person as the condition, or taking the ordinary person as the cause and the sage as the condition; even in the absence of strength or weakness, they may still function interchangeably."

Why is this? From the perspective of the capacity (the seeker), the capacity is intimate while the response is distant; from the perspective of the response, the response is intimate while the capacity is distant. Thus, they are reciprocally given different names.

However, the names "response" and "stimulus" cannot be established interchangeably. Although the great causal conditions (mahā-pratyaya) reside within the Trace Gate (jiamen), according to principle, both the Origin (ben) and the Trace (ji) must be indicated together; yet, since the Buddha’s appearance in the world is primarily for the purpose of revealing the Reality (shi), we shall for now follow the perspective of the Trace.
Furthermore, this is because [the text] yields to the fundamental and manifest aspects (honji-suijaku).
In the commentary, first the incorrect [view] is presented;
next, from "the true aspect" (*shissō*) onwards, the correct [view] is revealed.

Regarding the initial point that the middle [section] does not distinguish between the Bodhisattvas of the three vehicles but only excludes those of the human, celestial, and Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) realms, this is fully detailed in the *Xuánwén* (Text on the Profound).
Whether following the difficult points or the essential principles, subsequent sections follow this same pattern.

Regarding the statement that "it does not constitute a stimulus for the capacity [of those with limited faculties]," this is because it is not due to the extensive *dharmatā* (real nature) and *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination) of the present sutra.

Next, to clarify what is meant by "medium": since the meaning is already sufficient by contrasting the single great *dharmatā* against the small principle, there is no occasion to further elaborate on distinctions such as "equality" or "comprehensiveness. Furthermore, just as it is called "great," it should also be called "profound."

Regarding the statement, "The Buddha designates this as a 'phenomenon' (vastu)": in principle, it is not called a phenomenon; rather, because the Buddha wishes to use this principle to transform people, he names it a phenomenon. Because it consists of that which transforms and that which is transformed, it is termed "causes and conditions" (hetu-pratyaya).
Regarding the subsequent section on verifying through scripture: first is the direct citation;
second, from "It should be known" onwards, is the summary of the scriptural intent;
third, from "The Great Sūtra" onwards, is the re-citation.

Regarding the initial "correct citation," the term "various" (zhongzhong) implies that its meaning encompasses the entire dispensation; however, this would not necessarily be the case if it were intended for other schools.
As for "the Buddha-way," this specifically refers to the present teaching; therefore, from this point onward, the intent is directed toward this [teaching].

Next, regarding the "binding of the intention": "subtle" refers to the minor virtues of humans and devas at the initial stage of the various teachings; "manifest" refers to the fruits and virtues of those same teachings. Since both the subtle and the manifest—whether provisional or ultimate—are intended solely for manifestation, they are called "the fish-trap and the rabbit-snare."
The various expressions, whether subtle or manifest, must rely upon the eight teachings to reveal the four flavors as the *amṛta* (ghee); thus, the trap and the snare serve this purpose.

Therefore, both the trap and the snare are metaphors for that which enables penetration; the provisional teachings and provisional sections are established as the means to catch the single fish of ultimate reality and release it.
Alternatively, it may mean "hoof. The *Cangjie pian* states:
"It refers to the equipment for catching rabbits."
The *Zhuangzi* says: "One attains freedom from forgetting the trap.
This character for "trap" (*ti*) is used according to contemporary vernacular usage; the *Shuowen Jiezi* writes it as "die" (*di*).
If one says that the hoof is the foot, the expressive term [of "foot"] would not be established.
If one says that the hoof is the track, the meaning is likewise remote.
How could the principle of "seeking the track to escape" be so?
Now, one must follow the underlying meaning and take "jia" (罤) as the correct character.

Next, regarding the citation of the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (大經), this citation from that *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* serves to further substantiate the present section; it takes the single reality (*eka-tattva*) as the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), while the coarse and soft flavors must be understood as referring to the four flavors of provisional and real teachings.
Regarding the citation of evidence concerning the original and the trace, there are three parts:
first, concerning the teacher; second, concerning the disciples; third, the conclusion. The first section further contains two parts: [The text continues with the specific content of the first part.]
First, the main text is cited directly;
next, from "expedient means" (*upāya*) onwards, the text concerning the traces (*vyañjana*) is cited.
This is because this passage within the section on the traces implicitly reveals the intended meaning of the fundamental reality (*mūla*).
If one speaks of the manifest [teaching], it refers to the "trace" within the "trace-and-origin" (jike) framework; as will be clarified below, this text is universally applicable for citation.

Regarding the term "disciple," this also serves to reveal the Master by citing the subordinate, for if even the disciple is not truly minor, one can verify that the Master has not recently attained realization. Although those of sharp faculties may already know [the truth], they must await Maitreya’s prompting; thus, when they behold their original retinue and hear the teaching, they understand it without doubt.

Regarding the phrase "and so forth," the details are provided extensively in the subsequent text; it also serves to rebuke various masters of both ancient and modern times who do not even know that their own teacher’s fundamental and manifested traces (*honji-suijaku*), as well as his causes and effects, are uniquely transcendent among all teachings, let alone [understand] those of his disciples.

Furthermore, while the various scriptures of our disciples may contain such figures as Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara, the long-standing source for the Master’s [teachings] originates from the present sutra;
this is proven by the fact that the contemplation of the mind was first introduced therein.
Next, the section beginning with "You should know" concludes the intended meaning.

Regarding the initial passage: the *Śāriputra-abhidharma-śāstra* merely records that Śāriputra spoke [this] out of faith; in terms of its underlying principle, it is equivalent to having seen the Buddha.
This is because what you have spoken must have been heard from the Buddha, and those capable of hearing it must be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas.
Therefore, hearing your discourse is itself seeing the Buddha and so forth.

To summarize the meaning next: that which is heard is the Dharma; within the observing mind, this is precisely what is called the Buddha, and in this sense it is equivalent to seeing the Buddha. That which is the content of the mind is the disciples and so forth.
One immediately realizes within one's own mind that the Three Jewels are of one essence; this principle is perfectly complete, as detailed in the passage following "Having Heard and Spoken.

The note "and so forth" indicates that one is about to turn toward the meaning of contemplation, wherein, in contrast to what follows "Having Heard and Spoken," everything is contained within a single thought-moment.

Furthermore, if one is to be complete, one should clarify the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) by way of causes and conditions and by way of the original and trace aspects of the teachings. Thus, there are three contemplations corresponding to the objects and conditions; these involve the objects of the Three Jewels according to the principles of various teachings, where the contemplation of the Original is primary and the contemplation of the Trace is secondary, as well as the application and opening [of the gates], which can be understood through reflection.

Regarding "Manifesting the Signs," this refers specifically to the four types of signs shown in the present sutra. Although all sections—from the beginning with "Thus have I heard" to the end with "departed"—employ these four meanings, the application varies according to the structural progression of the text. For example, in explaining the General Introduction, each sentence requires all four [meanings], as it universally permeates both the Main Teaching and the Dissemination.
In explaining the Main Teaching, there are three [meanings] for both the Original and the Traces, though the principle applies to all four types.
In explaining the Dissemination, one must likewise possess all four, as it comprehensively encompasses the Main Teaching.

Furthermore, within the main body of the text, since the "Trace Gate" (Jikimon) lacks the distinction between the distant origin and the trace, the categories of essence and function (tai-yū) and origin and trace (hon-jaku) are borrowed; thus, none of the four names are omitted.

Moreover, regarding the provisional teachings in the Introduction (Jo), one must examine the textual flow: if it is necessary to distinguish them according to the five periods, then the teaching is already included therein;
if it is necessary to distinguish them according to the various teachings, then the periods are used as the criterion for judgment.

Regarding the provisional teachings (*kyō*) within the "Manifestation" (Jungzhong), one proceeds by clarifying the opening [of the truth] exclusively; regarding the provisional teachings within the "Fundamental" (Benzhong), one does not judge according to the teachings, but merely points out that the distant origin and the distant wondrousness are self-evident.

If one understands this text, then the entire sutra will be as clear as looking at one's own fingers and palms; the fourfold intention for its exegesis will be resolved without the need for further reflection. Therefore, for now, I shall provisionally rely on these three major sections of the text to generally demonstrate their characteristics; once the general understanding is attained, one should then apply this principle in detail to analyze each part individually.

In the initial section on causes and conditions (*nidāna*), there was no opportunity to examine each category in detail; for now, we shall merely indicate the three stages: planting the seed, ripening, and liberation.
Nevertheless, these three—planting the seed and so forth—must also be distinguished by means of the three factors of sequence and so on.

If there were only the introduction and so forth, there would be no distinction between the stages of past and future causes and effects; if there were only the seeds and so forth, there would be nothing from which hearing [the Dharma] proceeds, because the benefits derived from the three [seeds, etc. differ according to the three [stages of the introduction, etc. from which they proceed.

Furthermore, as in the introduction, the general preface pertains to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, while the specific preface pertains to the present. If the Buddha were still in the world, there would be five distinct stages within the specific preface, each adding further distinctions. As it is said regarding the *Anantamukha-sūtra*, there are three different types of secret benefits—seed, etc.—which are not the same; thus, one can observe that the seeing of light, the awakening through movement, and the receiving of flowers, as well as even the questions and answers, likewise possess these three types of benefits: seed, etc. This is how it should be understood.

Since the various chapters concerning the original and the trace differ throughout the text, even the general and specific introductions—extending to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when they were entrusted to those who propagate the teaching and encouraged to uphold, recite, and explain them—possess various categories; how much more so, then, for the main body of the teaching?
Therefore, by resorting to these two or three [categories], one may gain an understanding of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).

First, regarding the "seeds" (*bīja*) and so forth: it is necessary to rely on the characteristics of the teachings (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*) in order to distinguish between existence and non-existence; thus, the length of the causal conditions varies across the various teachings.

For example, according to those who follow the Tripiṭaka, during the three great kalpas and one hundred kalpas, one merely cultivates the six pāramitās for oneself to nourish the body of merit and adorn it with the marks and signs, while establishing karmic conditions with sentient beings as seeds to bring them to maturity and liberation.

Regarding the self-cultivation of the initial stage of the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*), one nears the seventh ground by retaining afflictions (*kleśa*) to sustain rebirth and form karmic conditions with sentient beings; this is called "first planting the seeds.
Upon entering extinction according to these two teachings, there is no transformation in the future; rather, beings are matured and liberated only at the time of attaining Buddhahood.

The authority of teaching (*śāsana*) and the authority of principle (*tattva*) are not the intended meaning of this sutra; even the first stage (*bhūmi*) of the Separate Teaching (*pratyekabuddha-yāna*) is still able to possess them, let alone the fulfillment of the fruit.

Although the Separate Teaching possesses these, its teaching remains ultimately provisional (*upāya*). How much more so when there is the fundamental cause and the distant planting of seeds? Furthermore, the two gates of "Original" (*mūla*) and "Trace" (*liṅga*) through which this sutra applies its transformation differ from other sutras; for these four sections of the text, there is indeed a profound reason.
Therefore, among the four sections, only the first two are called the "primary retinue.
Although the first section is detached and exists in the present, it is still designated as the primary retinue because it fully conveys the original seeds.
The reason it is not stated here that these are the "original" [seeds] is that they are all equally being liberated for the first time at this present moment.

As for those whose original seeds are near liberation, because Maitreya did not recognize them and thus gave rise to doubt, they specifically receive the name "original. However, as for those currently being liberated, if they have not yet attained the Buddha-wisdom, they are still unable to know their seeds; this [text] merely sets forth their intended meaning.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the elucidation of the three [factors] beginning with the seed; second, the elucidation of the three beginning with the sequence.
The first section has four parts:
First, the causes and conditions are explicitly elucidated;
second, from "Although not yet... onwards, doubts are resolved;
third, from "In the interval... onwards, the causes and conditions are explained in terms of the three periods and nine periods of time.
4. From "For what reason" onwards, the text cites evidence for the causal conditions of the three periods and nine periods.

The initial passage consists of four sections that demonstrate these characteristics; the first section concerns the original seeds of cause and fruit, which ripen only after the fruit has matured, at which point one is liberated in the royal city.
Next, regarding the section beginning with "Furthermore," the seeds of the original cause ripen near the end of the fruit, and one is immediately liberated upon passing into another world.

As for the reference to those who emerge from the earth, we know that those described as "original retinues" who emerge from the earth are actually those whose original seeds are only now being liberated in the present age;
since Maitreya does not recognize them, they are not [liberated] in the most immediate sense.
Next are those who planted [the seeds] in the intermediate period; having matured through past teachings, they attain liberation today.
Next, from the section beginning with "Furthermore," are those who plant [the seeds] today, which will mature in the future and lead to liberation in the future.

These four sections merely capture the general outline; from the original cause and original fruit down to the intermediate period, the recent past, and the present, how could there be only these four sections? They extend vertically in depth and horizontally in breadth even unto the future, continuing eternally and without end.

If it were not so, there would be present effects without causes and present causes without effects; this would revert to the nihilism of total annihilation, wherein transformation has neither beginning nor end. Therefore, one should know that while the stages unfold in infinite layers upon layers, they ultimately take the three sections of the Buddha Vehicle as their foundation, with the three teachings for humans and devas serving to assist in their manifestation.
The section beginning with "Although not yet... serves to resolve doubts.
Here, the causes and conditions are clarified; according to the sequence of the text, they should properly be situated within the *jì* (trace) aspect.

To explore and restrict the discussion to the intermediate stage of the *běn-dì* (original ground) is precisely to simultaneously indicate both the *běn* (origin) and the *jì* (trace), thereby manifesting the characteristics of this entire treatise. This adopts the purport of the subsequent text and the purport of the methods of transformation (*huà-yí*).

Next, regarding the "three periods and nine periods," this is fully explained in the first fascicle of the *Zhi guan* commentary, which cites the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Śrīgarbha-vyūha-sūtra*. Thus, one should know that throughout the future limit, the three periods and nine periods consist of the three stages of planting, ripening, and liberation. This means that in every thought-moment there are the three mysteries, the three nines, the three segments, the inverse and the direct, and the body and the land; each of these is distinct, yet each enters into reality.
Regarding the fourth point, citing the original text as proof, this serves to verify the existence of the three periods of time.

If there are three periods, then there are nine periods; since the nine are merely the three, this first provides general verification for the broad principle of the three periods. By extension, the three periods within every single thought-moment can be understood according to this same analogy.

The supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) belong to the past; however, the meaning of "supernormal power" actually penetrates all three periods of time, as it is distinguished from the other two [categories].

"Lion" represents the present and "majestic ferocity" represents the future. This is intended to make known that the Buddha’s transformative conditions extend far; thus, returning to the original text, he cites the distant to encompass the near, thereby proving the four sections.
The section beginning with "By means of this" concerns the three [sections], starting with the Introduction (nidāna).

The initial passage first refers generally to both types of introductions; therefore, it says that the introductory portion is universally applicable because there is nothing specific to be indicated.

Below the phrase "the multitude beheld," there is a specific reference to the introductory section; because it serves as the cause for generating the correct [understanding], it says, "the multitude beheld something rare.
"Yǒngyǒng" means to look up with reverence.
"From 'The Buddha responds to the capacity' below is the Main Teaching (Zhengzong).
From 'Not only... below, it correctly clarifies that the Main Teaching is the foundation for its circulation.

Since these three sections all pertain to the innate seeds and so forth, one knows that every word, every phrase, every assembly, every flavor, and every lifetime and every thought-moment constantly functions for sentient beings as the planting, ripening, and liberation of the Single Buddha Vehicle."

This text follows the general judgment of our own school for now: when Śākyamuni preached this sūtra as he did, both the general fivefold and the specific fivefold [factors] were none other than causes and conditions—namely, the causes and conditions for the certification of faith (*śraddhā-pratītyasamutpāda*) and the causes and conditions for the initiation [of the teaching].
Furthermore, this encompasses both the general conditions for the fivefold harmony and the specific conditions for their sequential order.
Thus, from the preliminary stages through to the main practice until the attainment of liberation, it is said: "Opening, showing, awakening, and entering."

Aside from those already delivered, all others are yet to be ripened; therefore, for those who have not yet attained liberation, it is essential that this teaching circulate. Thus it is said that the wondrous Way reaches far and wide, and all of this is the responsive manifestation of this very sutra.
Regarding the phrase "the final five hundred years," if one follows the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, it simply lists five hundred years as follows:

in the first hundred years, liberation will be firm; in the second hundred years, meditative concentration will be firm; in the third hundred years, the observance of precepts will be firm; in the fourth hundred years, extensive learning will be firm; and in the fifth hundred years, generosity will be firm.
Regarding the phrase "the final hundred years of the latter five-hundred-year period," some say that according to the *Mahāsannipāta-sūtra*,

there are five periods of five hundred years each; the first through the fourth are the same as previously described, while only the fifth five-hundred-year period is said to be characterized by the persistence of strife and contention (*raṇa-dṛḍha*).
The phrase "the latter five hundred" refers to the final five hundred years.
If one were to discuss the five hundred alone, it would still fall within the period of the True Dharma (*saddharma*).

Although this deviates slightly from the formal treatises and its reasoning is somewhat obscured, let us for the moment follow the convention of "five times five hundred. At the beginning of the Final Dharma (*mappō*), there is still no lack of those who attain both the hidden and manifest benefits; thus, based on the time when the Great Teaching can still circulate, it is called "five hundred."
Therefore, the three elements—the introduction and so forth—are nothing other than manifestations of resonance and response.

Regarding the phrase "furthermore, showing the characteristics of the teaching": it is called the "characteristics of the teaching" because they pertain to the nature of the teaching; the differentiation of the five flavors is for the purpose of revealing the *amṛta* (the finest essence), and generally speaking, all sacred words bestowed upon those below are collectively termed "teaching."
Now, this teaching has the distinct merit of revealing the ultimate reality; therefore, it is called "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*).
Furthermore, it separately demonstrates the characteristics of the *amṛta* (the supreme nectar) by means of three stages;

therefore, it is called "characteristics. Thus, within each of the three stages, the partial and the Hinayana are excluded. This constitutes, for the time being, a single type of three-stage structure, deferring the distinction between the "Original" (*hon*) and the "Trace" (*jaku*) to what follows; for this reason, two types of three-stage structures have not yet been differentiated.
Question:
If that is so, how does this differ from the three sections on causes and conditions mentioned previously? Answer:
Previously, I briefly addressed the three periods in relation to those who respond to the teachings to clarify the seeds and so forth;

now, I shall comprehensively distinguish the methods of the shallow and deep applications of what has been taught. Therefore, I will briefly summarize the four teachings to discern the three stages; yet, when investigated to the ultimate point, these are still simply the three stages of the wondrous principle of causes and conditions.

Moreover, when observing that both the mind and its manifestations—both the fundamental and the phenomenal—belong entirely to the realm of causes and conditions, the details regarding the characteristics of the teachings are fully set forth in the *Mysterious* (Xuán) Text. First, the coarse is determined by means of relative dependence; next, the subtle is distinguished by means of absolute transcendence.
Question:

Regarding the five meanings of the general introduction (*sūtra-pūrvapīṭhikā*) and the "Flower Land" of the specific introduction (*sūtra-uttarapīṭhikā*), these are merely matters of fact; how can all three sections be termed "instruction through demonstration" (*nidarśana-deśanā*)? Answer:

In general discourse, all [elements] constitute the correct exposition of the preceding characteristics; in specific discourse, only the questions and answers constitute the teaching. Furthermore, according to the general explanation, there is nothing that does not manifest the teaching; therefore, the text briefly states: "This is not a preface for the sake of humans or devas," and so forth.
"The Two Vehicles" refers to the Tripitaka teaching;
"immediately realizing emptiness" refers to the Shared Teaching;
and "exclusively for Bodhisattvas" refers to the Distinct Teaching.
The phrase "uprightness," and so forth, reveals the provisional teachings.
The sections on the "Correct" [Teaching] and the "Circulation" [of the Sūtra] may be understood accordingly.
Regarding "the glow of a firefly," the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"A bodhisattva practicing *prajñā* for a single day outshines fireflies as the sun illuminates the world.
This passage criticizes the Tripiṭaka [teachings], and thus uses the lamp and torch as metaphors for the Shared (Tongjiao) teaching.

The lamp is like the two vehicles, and the torch is like the bodhisattvas; although both possess *prajñā*, there is no lack of distinction between clarity and obscurity. The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) is what differentiates them.
Regarding "like the stars and the moon": those before the stages (*bhūmi*) are like the stars, while those who have ascended to the stages are like the moon.
Therefore, although the stars possess bright light, it does not reach far, because they allow things distant to be seen;
although ordinary wisdom illuminates, it does not reach the clarity of the sages, because its mind is limited;
and the moon does not equal the sun, because it merely carries forth the path of teaching.
Furthermore, one should also clarify the sequence and non-sequence of the three wisdoms and the three truths to manifest the characteristics of the teaching; this is not urgent at present.
Regarding the phrase "bambu leaves" and so forth, it refers to the meaning of the "Chapter on the Infant’s Conduct" (*Dārakavratapatala*) in the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Regarding the fact that the current text briefly mentions only humans and devas: although the term "infant" (ārbhaka) has a broad application across various teachings, it is here used to refer specifically to humans and devas because they represent the most limited [capacity].

However, the parable in that sutra proceeds from the sudden toward the gradual; its initial statement that [the infant] cannot rise, sit, come, go, or speak refers to the perfect (or *pariniṣpanna*) infant.
The "large characters" refer to the *pitaka* (the Canon).
"Not knowing suffering, pleasure, and so forth" refers to the *āgama* (the Discourses).
The phrase "below" indicates the distinctions between the large and small [vehicles].
Those who weep and so forth are humans and devas.
Since the sutra generally refers to those with minor wholesome roots as "infants," the stage of the perfect cause is also called "infancy.
As the sutra says:
"The 'half-syllables' refer to the nine divisions [of the scriptures];
the 'full-syllables' refer to the *Vyākaraṇa*, which is here called the 'Root of Letters. Hexi said:

"The root of all worldly scripts, though belonging to external treatises, contains no heterodox teachings; as it was not composed by Bodhisattvas, it may be compared to the twelve divisions of the Mahāyāna sūtras."

The ancients knew only the one great vehicle of the Vaipulya (Prajñā) gate; nowadays it is not so, for having distinguished between the common and the specific, we take only the Perfect gate to be the fulfillment.
This is what is meant by "relying on the meaning and not on the words."
